These overlap somewhat with Fullers three functions, but they do tease 
out specific advantages to written agreements that 
are imperfectly 
captured by Fuller's categories. 
Each of these functions furthers some aspect of contracting behavior, 
but none of them does so without a cost. Critics of the Statute of Frauds 
argue that these costs far exceed any benefits the Statute yields. The 
most obvious cost is the cost of preparing and executing the writing, a 
cost incurred whether a contract really needed to be in writing or not. 
Another cost arises if a contract actually was formed but s rendered 
unenforceable by the Statute of Frauds, thus defeating the xpectations 
of at least one party to the contract. Indeed, the Statute of Frauds may 
even be used to produce fraud. If one party to a contract knows that the 
contract falls within the Statute of Frauds and the other doesn't, the 
more knowledgeable party may prefer to keep the contract oral. If the 
contract is profitable, then that party will perform; if it is le ; profitable 
than some alternative, that party may choose not to pcrfo n and will 
then assert the Statute of Frauds as a defense. (Ethical issw s may arise 
from using this "technical" defense, especially if the defend nt's lawyer 
knows that the parties really did make a contract but that t e Statute of 
Frauds would bar its enforcement. These are discussed in Section Six 
below.)
